title: Ex 8.12 · Removing an intersection
prompt: Let $A$, $B$ and $C$ be any sets. Prove that $A - (B \cap C) = (A - B) \cup (A - C)$.
answer_format: A chain of lines, each a set (like A ∪ (B ∩ C)) or a statement about an element x (like x ∈ A or x ∈ B). Each line must have exactly the same elements as the line before; start from the left side and end at the right side.
hints: x ∈ A − (B ∩ C) means x ∈ A and x ∉ B ∩ C.
x ∉ B ∩ C is not (x ∈ B and x ∈ C). De Morgan's law turns this into x ∉ B or x ∉ C.
Distribute 'x ∈ A and' over the 'or'. Each piece (x ∈ A and x ∉ B) is x ∈ A − B.
solution: Let $x$ be any element. Then $x \in A - (B \cap C)$ means $x \in A \land \sim(x \in B \land x \in C)$.

By De Morgan's law this is $x \in A \land (x 
otin B \lor x 
otin C)$, and by the distributive law it is $(x \in A \land x 
otin B) \lor (x \in A \land x 
otin C)$.
That says $x \in A - B$ or $x \in A - C$, so $x \in (A - B) \cup (A - C)$.
Every step was an equivalence, so $A - (B \cap C) = (A - B) \cup (A - C)$. $\blacksquare$

reference.note: This exact exercise, restated in ProofLab's words. Uses Section 8.3 (proving A = B), the definitions of union, intersection and difference (Section 1.5) and the logic laws of Section 2.6.

steps.content: x ∈ A and x ∉ B ∩ C
x ∈ A and not (x ∈ B and x ∈ C)
x ∈ A and (x ∉ B or x ∉ C)
(x ∈ A and x ∉ B) or (x ∈ A and x ∉ C)
x ∈ A − B or x ∈ A − C
x ∈ A and not (x ∈ B and x ∈ C)
x ∈ A and (x ∉ B and x ∉ C)
